## TL;DR

I ran a headless browser pass on the Deployments page at 1280px and 375px using the auth-less server launched from a scratch worktree. The binding state, deploy confirmation, and refused-push presentation all fit without horizontal overflow. I added a deterministic refused-push capture fixture and component coverage for both the fixture and the deploy error interaction, and documented the observed results in `docs/qa/2026-11-deployments-flows.md`.

## Work and rationale

I started by checking the task's current branch and clean state, reading the task specification, and tracing the Deployments view, its existing component tests, and the shot-fixture registry. The page already represented the service-by-branch matrix, deployment branch state, local environment binding, and the important caveat that a recent Git change does not prove the provider finished a successful build. Existing tests covered cached data, refresh failures, member/admin access, local-only environment binding, branch synchronization, and the configured/empty page state.

The gap was around the deploy confirmation and failure path. There was no named fixture that opened a refused deployment in its confirmation dialog, and there was no component test proving the dialog stays open when the deploy API rejects. That state matters because losing the branch and command context after a refused push would make recovery less clear. I added `deployments:deployFailure` as a preview-only fixture, reusing the existing fake Dashboard deployment data and opening the production-branch confirmation with an explicit divergence message. It does not invoke the API or touch a remote.

I added one test for the fixture's dialog and alert with no API calls, plus one test that exercises the actual view behavior when the deploy request rejects. The latter checks that the error appears and the confirmation remains available. I also wrote a QA note that records the exact view states, viewport checks, and limits of the mocked run.

For browser QA, I created an isolated scratch worktree under the assigned worktree, linked its dependencies to the already-installed branch dependencies, and ran `just serve-noauth` there. Playwright ran headlessly against that server. I inspected screenshots for the environment binding at mobile width and the refused-push dialog at mobile width. Both had no horizontal overflow. The dialog remained legible and all three actions (close, retry, cancel) stayed visible.

## Approaches tried

I first ran the page's pre-existing environment-binding fixture at both required widths and opened the deploy confirmation. This confirmed the layout and command copy before adding anything. Then I intercepted the deploy endpoint in Playwright to return HTTP 409 with a realistic divergence message. The page displayed the error in an alert while keeping the confirmation open and preserving the command context. That interaction worked, so the change was focused on making the scenario reproducible and covered in regression tests rather than changing already-correct presentation behavior.

The initial focused test run exposed two harness details: fixture type validation reads the built core fixture module, so a rebuild was needed after registering the new state; and the confirmation uses Vue Teleport, which places dialog content in `document.body` outside the component wrapper. I adjusted the test queries to match the rendered DOM and reran the focused tests successfully.

## Challenges and blockers

The auth-less server is required to run from a scratch worktree, not the active worktree or a checkout that might have a real RepoOS server. The new fixture existed only in the active branch's uncommitted source, so I copied the two relevant source files into the isolated scratch copy before rebuilding and restarting it. This kept the browser server separate while allowing the final fixture to be exercised.

The browser failure was intentionally simulated. It verifies the UI response to a failed request but cannot verify provider credentials, a real remote push, or provider build success. No external deployment was attempted, and no live secret or account data was used.

## Key learnings

The Deployments page's mobile layout stacks service details into readable cards, and the deployment failure UI preserves the confirmation context rather than replacing it. A named shot fixture plus component tests gives future reviewers a reliable way to inspect this error without creating a real deployment. In this repository, when a UI test depends on a fixture imported through a `.js` path, rebuild before trusting the fixture result; and for teleported UI, assert against the document body rather than only the Vue wrapper.

The QA result is therefore limited but useful: layout, copy, and failure-state handling passed under deterministic local conditions. Actual provider build status continues to be checked through each provider's dashboard, as the UI already explains.
